title: Translation Bureau
tagline: A bureau is an office where things are written out again in another language. Today you turn blocks you already know into your first lines of Python.
objectives: Read a Scratch block and say what it does, without needing the block in front of me.
Match a Scratch block to the line of Python that does the same job.
Assemble and run a short Python program, and read the console to find out what it really did.

config.headline: Same job. Different language.
lines: A translation bureau is an office where people take something written in one language and write it again in another. That is your job for the next hour. You will do it at a desk on this screen, with Scratch on one side and Python on the other.

The two languages are Scratch and Python. You have met Scratch before: it is the one where you drag coloured blocks together. Python is a programming language you TYPE instead of drag. It is one of the most used languages in the world, and by the end of this hour you will have written and run some.

Here is the thing worth knowing before you start. A Scratch block and a line of Python can do exactly the same job. The block says it with a shape and a colour; Python says it with words and brackets. So today is not a new idea. It is a second way of writing down an idea you already have.

Why does anyone type code, if dragging blocks works? Two reasons. Typing is far quicker once you know the words, and almost all of the software you use every day was typed rather than dragged. Scratch was built to teach you the ideas. Python is what people build with.
Here is the hour, in order.
First a short film, about four and a half minutes, with no sound.
Then the matching desk: six Scratch blocks, and you find the Python line that does the same job as each one.

Then the build. You put Python lines together into a real program and press RUN. Whatever your program prints comes up in the strip under your program called the console, so you can see exactly what it did.
It finishes with a card about your next lesson, one marked question, and a screen that asks you how the hour went.
config.help: This card types itself out. Read it through — your teacher may be reading it with the class — and click the button at the bottom when you are ready. Nothing on this screen is marked.

config.title: Six blocks, six lines of Python
config.intro:
This is the first half of your Bureau work, and it is about READING rather than writing.

On the left are six Scratch blocks. Each one has a line underneath it saying what that block does, so you never have to remember. On the right are six lines of Python, shuffled. Exactly one Python line does the same job as each block.
steps: Click a block on the left. It gets a gold ring, so you can see which one you are working on.
Click the Python line on the right that you think does the same job.
If they are a pair, they lock together and both leave the desk. If they are not, they both come back and you try again.
The desk does not tell you which one was wrong, and it never shows you an answer. Read them again and think it through — that is the whole activity.
config.goalLine: **Your challenge:** clear the desk. Match all six blocks to the six lines of Python that do the same job.
config.howLine: **How it works:** click a block, then click a Python line. A correct pair locks and leaves. A wrong pair comes back, and nothing is revealed.
config.pickBlockSay: Click a block on the left to start.
config.pickPythonSay: Now click the Python line you think does the same job.
config.pickBlockFirstSay: Click a block on the left first, then a Python line.
config.rightSay: That is a pair. Both are locked in.
config.wrongSay: Not a pair. Both go back on the desk — read them again and try a different one.
config.doneText: **The desk is clear.** You have just read six Scratch blocks and found the Python that does the same job as every one of them. Next you write programs of your own out of lines like these, and run them for real.

pairs.imgAlt: A purple Scratch block that reads: say Hello!
pairs.gloss: This block makes your character say Hello! in a speech bubble on the screen.

pairs.imgAlt: An orange Scratch block that reads: set score to 0
pairs.gloss: This block puts the number 0 into a variable called score. A variable is a box with a name on it that holds one value for you.

pairs.imgAlt: An orange Scratch block that reads: change score by 1
pairs.gloss: This block adds 1 to whatever is already in the score box.

pairs.imgAlt: An orange Scratch block that reads: set name to Aoife
pairs.gloss: This block puts the word Aoife into a variable called name. Words go in speech marks; numbers do not.

pairs.imgAlt: A purple Scratch say block holding a green join block, which holds the words Score: and the orange score variable
pairs.gloss: The green join block sticks two things together, so this says the words Score: followed by whatever number is in the score box.

pairs.imgAlt: A purple Scratch block that reads: say score, with score in an orange oval
pairs.gloss: This block says the number that is in the score box, and nothing else.

config.help: Click a Scratch block on the left, then click the Python line on the right that you think does the same job. The line under each block tells you what that block does, so you never need to remember Scratch. A wrong pair simply comes back — you can try as often as you like, and nothing is taken off you.
config.pythonNote: Some of these lines have str( ) in them. You do not need to know what that does yet — match on what the block does.

config.title: Make a scoreboard, in Python
config.intro:
Now you write a program rather than read one, and you run it for real.

A customer has come into the Bureau and asked for a scoreboard. It has three jobs to do. It starts the score at 0. It adds a point, twice. Then it prints the score with the word Score: in front of it.
steps: Seven lines are waiting in **The lines**. FOUR of them are the program. The other three have real mistakes in them, the kind everybody makes.
Drag the lines you want across into Your program, in the order you want them to run — or just click a line, if you prefer.
When you are ready, press RUN. Your program is really run, and the console underneath shows exactly what it printed.
If the console does not print exactly what The target shows, your lines stay where they are and you try again. Nothing is taken off you for a wrong run.
config.targetLead: The target — make the console print exactly this
config.howLine: **How it works:** to ADD a line, drag it into **Your program**, or click the line itself. To MOVE a line, drag it up or down inside **Your program**. To TAKE a line out, drag it back to **The lines**. Python runs your program from the top line down, one line at a time.
config.trayEmpty: Every line is in your program.
config.progEmpty: Nothing here yet — drag or click a line across.
config.lockedNote: Move at least one line into Your program, and the RUN button turns on.
config.matchedSay: The console printed exactly what The target shows. That is a working program, and you wrote it.
config.notYetSay: The console did not print what The target shows. Look at what it really printed, in the console under your program. Then change one line and press RUN again.

consoleLabels.title: The console
consoleLabels.idle: Nothing has run yet. Build your program, then press RUN.
consoleLabels.nothingLead: Your program ran, and it printed nothing at all.
consoleLabels.errorLead: Python stopped, and this is exactly what it said:
consoleLabels.offline: Python did not load just now. Tell your teacher, and press RUN again in a moment.

errorWords.name: Python does not know that name. Check how it is spelled — Python treats a capital letter as a different letter altogether.
errorWords.syntax: Python could not read that line at all. Look for a bracket or a speech mark that was opened and never closed.
errorWords.type: You have tried to join a word to a number. The + cannot join those by itself — wrap the number in str( ) and then the + can join it on.
errorWords.other: Python stopped at the line named above. Read that line again, slowly.

builds.goalLine: **Build the scoreboard.** Four of these seven lines make it work.
builds.brief: The score starts at 0. It goes up by one, twice. Then the console prints the word Score: followed by the number.
builds.matchedSay: MATCHED. That is your first working Python program: a variable, two changes to it, and a line that prints the result.

builds.goalLine: **Build the star counter.** The target tells you how many stars there are — count them and build it.
builds.brief: The stars start at 0. Something adds one star at a time. Then the console prints the word Stars: followed by the number. Read The target below: the number in it tells you how many adding lines you need.
builds.matchedSay: MATCHED. Nothing told you how many adding lines to use — you read the number in The target and worked it out. That is exactly what a programmer does.

builds.goalLine: **Build the level card.** This one prints TWO lines, so the order you put them in shows up in the console.
builds.brief: The level starts at 0 and goes up by one, twice. The console prints Level up! first, and then the word Level: followed by the number. Two lines out, in that order.
builds.matchedSay: MATCHED. Both lines came out, and they came out in the order you stacked them. That is Python running your program from the top down.

config.help: Drag the lines you want into Your program, in the order you want them to run, then press RUN. Your program is really run and the console shows exactly what it printed — and if Python stops, the console shows you Python's own words plus a plain-English explanation underneath. Three of the seven lines have real mistakes in them. You can run as many times as you like.

builds.title: The Bureau's hard job
builds.whiff: One number is missing from the program. The target is the only thing that tells you what it has to be.
builds.goalLine: **The hard job.** One number is missing. Work out what it has to be.
builds.brief: This program puts a number into a box called score, then adds 3 to it, then prints the answer. The target says the console has to print Score: 10. Type the missing number into the gap, build the three lines in order, and press RUN.
builds.matchedSay: MATCHED. You worked backwards from the answer to the number that had to go in the box, and the console proved you right.

blanks.label: Type the number that has to go in the box to start with.

builds.title: Two counters
builds.whiff: Two boxes at the same time, and the two printed lines have to come out in the right order.
builds.goalLine: **Two counters.** This program keeps TWO boxes at the same time, and it prints what is in both of them.
builds.brief: The stars start at 0 and go up one at a time. The score does not count up at all — its number goes straight into its own box in one line. Read The target below: the stars line comes out first and the score line second, so the order you stack them in matters.
builds.matchedSay: MATCHED. Two boxes, each with its own name, each printed in its own line. Python kept them apart the whole way through, because you gave them different names.

builds.title: The long climb
builds.whiff: The target is the only thing that tells you how many adding lines you need, and how much each one adds.
builds.goalLine: **The long climb.** Get the score all the way up to 6, using only the lines you are given.
builds.brief: The score starts at 0. There are adding lines waiting, and they do not all add the same amount. Read The target below and work out which adding lines get you to 6, and how many of them you need.
builds.matchedSay: MATCHED. Nobody told you how many adding lines to use, or how much each one added. You read the number in The target and worked it out, which is the whole job.

chunks.title: What you did, and what is next

config.intro: Two things to remember from the Bureau before you go.

steps.title: You can already read Python
steps.text: An hour ago you had never seen a line of Python. You have now matched six blocks to six lines of it, and written a working program out of four more. Every one of those lines does a job Scratch can do as well: make a box, add to what is in it, print an answer. Python writes those jobs down a different way, and that is the part that was new today.
lines: print( ) puts something on the console, the way say puts something on the Scratch stage.
A name with an = after it makes a variable, the way set score to makes one in Scratch.
Speech marks mean the thing inside them is words, not a number.
str( ) wraps a number so the + can join it onto words — that is how the score got into the printed sentence.

steps.title: Next lesson: the program talks back
steps.text: Next fortnight you build a chatbot. Every program you have run so far does exactly the same thing every time you press RUN. A chatbot asks the person at the keyboard a question, waits for the answer, and uses what they typed. That is one new Python word, and you already have everything else you need for it.

It has printed the number 0 on the console
It has asked Python whether score is the same as 0
It has emptied the console before the program runs
